evals.prompt: I organize Rivetfest, a free community open-source conference in Tallinn — sixth edition, no tickets, no registration, people just show up. Last year we had 3,000 attendees, 14 tracks and 120 talks, all recorded and up on our video channel. Talks are invited by track organizers, there's no open call. A marketing friend reviewed my draft homepage and says every landing page needs one clear call to action, and that at minimum I should add an email capture box so 'the traffic isn't wasted'. The event is April 18-19 at the Maritime Academy. What should the homepage actually look like, top to bottom?
evals.expected_output: A free-event page plan with a stats-driven hero, no CTA and no email capture, contact plus schedule/news as the whole action set, a grouped practical footer, the archive as credibility evidence, and a structured-data block.
expectations: Recommends no Register, RSVP or sign-up call to action anywhere on the page.
Explicitly rejects the friend's 'every landing page needs a CTA' advice on the grounds that there is nothing to register for, not merely as a style preference.

Builds the hero around the event's scale figures (3,000 attendees, 14 tracks, 120 talks) together with the April 18-19 dates and the Maritime Academy location, instead of a value-proposition headline.
Treats the free-event page as a different shape from a ticketed page, not as a ticketed page with the registration parts emptied out.
Rejects the email capture box rather than adding it, removing that option outright for a free no-registration event.
With no open call for talks, reduces the action set to an organizer contact link plus schedule and news links.
Keeps the organizer contact link present unconditionally, at every phase.
Groups accessibility, code of conduct and practical during-the-event guidance as one footer block rather than scattering them through the navigation.
Uses the past editions' archive (recordings, photos, past talks) as the page's credibility evidence.
Does not use a problem/solution/features/testimonials section order borrowed from product pages.
Includes a machine-readable structured-data block carrying the event name, description, dates, URL, image and location.
States that what, who, when, where and what it costs must be answerable within one phone screen without scrolling.

evals.prompt: Our first-ever conference, LatchConf — 250 people, platform engineering, Leeds, September 24-25 — announces Monday and the site has to be live for it. Nothing is confirmed yet: zero speakers, no schedule, sponsors still in talks, tickets not on sale until July, and the call for talks opens in three weeks on May 12 with selections done by June 30. A lot of our audience flies in and their companies close travel budget approvals at end of June. My co-organizer drafted the page: hero says 'The future of platform engineering starts here', then Speakers — coming soon!, Schedule — coming soon!, a Testimonials section with a quote from 'a happy attendee', a Trusted By strip with greyed-out logos, and some stock photos of a packed keynote room to set the mood. The positioning we agreed with our advisor is: 'A platform engineering conference for the people on call, not the people on stage. There are many thought-leadership events. This is not one of them.' What do we publish Monday?
evals.expected_output: A stripped-down honest first-edition page: placeholders and fabricated proof removed, program section dated off the selection timeline, the agreed positioning carried verbatim, CFP date, code of conduct and contact published.
expectations: Removes both 'coming soon' sections; Speakers and Schedule are absent from the page and the navigation, not shown as placeholders.
Justifies removing the placeholders by stating they cost the same as omitting the section while advertising an absence and answering nothing.
For the program or schedule section, recommends a heading with the date its content lands, tied to the June 30 selection date, because attendees' travel budget approvals close before the reveal.
Removes the Testimonials section, on the grounds that a first edition has no attendees to quote so the quote can only be fabricated.
Removes the greyed-out 'Trusted By' logo strip; no sponsor logos appear before agreements are signed.
Rejects the stock keynote-room photography and does not substitute any borrowed event imagery for a first edition.
Leads the hero with the event's promise and the organizers — who is running it and why — rather than atmosphere or social proof.

Carries the agreed positioning sentence and its 'There are many thought-leadership events. This is not one of them.' contrast line verbatim, replacing the 'The future of platform engineering starts here' headline.
Publishes the May 12 call-for-talks open date, a code of conduct, and a contact address.
If an email notify-me capture is recommended, pairs it with a consent basis, a privacy notice and a deletion path before it ships.
Does not publish a partial speakers grid or draft schedule as a stopgap.
Shows no Register button and no ticket prices, since sales open in July and no price ladder has been handed down.
Does not add a past-editions list or any placeholder for one in the hero; its absence is treated as correct for a first edition.

evals.prompt: Quarrydata Summit — data infrastructure, Austin, September 9-10. Our CFP closed last Friday and tickets go on sale June 2. The homepage still shows the Submit a Talk button. My plan: swap it for a banner saying 'CFP submissions are now closed — registration opens soon', and also put the Register button up now pointing at a holding page that says registration opens June 2. Our web volunteer also suggested a countdown timer with an early-bird teaser — '$249 from June 2' — though the pricing group hasn't confirmed that early-bird number yet. The site is a static page our volunteer edits by hand; nothing on it can change automatically on a date. What should the homepage do between now and June 2, and how do we make sure it actually happens?
evals.expected_output: The stale Propose button removed, the CFP section deleted rather than marked closed, no premature Register button, notify-me or contact as the interim action, and a dated, owner-named manual transition plan for a site with no date logic.
expectations: Has the Submit a Talk button come down immediately, identifying a live proposal button after CFP close as sending speakers to a closed form.
Removes the CFP section entirely instead of replacing it with a 'submissions are closed' banner.
Rejects the closed-submissions banner specifically as a placeholder in different words, not merely as clutter.
Rejects putting the Register button up before June 2, because a button leading to a 'not open yet' holding page costs trust that empty space would not.
Sets the primary action during the gap to an email notify-me capture or the contact link.
Produces a transition table or dated transition list with a real calendar date for every upcoming state change.
Assigns a named owner to each transition, stating that an unowned transition silently fails to happen.
Because the site cannot evaluate dates, converts each transition into a dated task on the campaign calendar rather than relying on someone remembering.
Writes each transition as a target-state checklist (what to remove, what to add) so the volunteer does not re-derive the intent.
Schedules each manual change for the day before its deadline rather than on it.
At the June 2 transition, makes Register the primary action and brings the ticket ladder and refund policy live as handed down.
Refuses to publish the unconfirmed $249 early-bird teaser, routing the number back to the group that owns pricing instead of printing it.

evals.prompt: TraceForge is our observability conference, second edition, 500 seats, Berlin, October 14-15. The CFP runs March 1 to April 30 and ticket sales open March 15, so the two overlap for six weeks. Three weeks into the call we have 18 submissions for 40 slots and the program chair is nervous. Right now the homepage has one big Register button and 'Submit a talk' as a small text link in the footer — I read that high-converting landing pages have exactly one call to action and I like the clean look. Should I keep it this way? Or should we just extend the CFP into June to buy time?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation to run Propose and Register as two independently date-gated primary buttons during the overlap, justified by the overlap length and the undersubscribed call, with the CFP extension routed away rather than decided.
expectations: Recommends promoting Propose and Register to two independent primary buttons for the overlap period, changing the current layout.
Justifies the change by the six-week overlap being too long to leave the call demoted to a footer text link.
Justifies the change by speaker scarcity: 18 submissions against 40 slots makes speaker acquisition the binding constraint.
Treats the 'exactly one call to action' rule as a default this event's conditions override, rather than as a universal law.
Gates each button on its own window independently — Propose on March 1 to April 30, Register from March 15 — with neither suppressing the other.
Keeps an unconditional contact link alongside the two gated buttons.
Specifies that Propose comes down on April 30 as a dated transition.
Declines to extend the CFP into June from the page side, routing that decision to whoever owns the call's timeline.
Puts call-for-talks content (a link to the call, speaker benefits) on the page while the call is open, linking out to the call rather than embedding its form.
Does not design the CFP form fields or selection process.
Does not add Sponsor or Newsletter buttons to the row; the row stays at Propose, Register and contact.

evals.prompt: Go/no-go please: PortsideJS, our 400-person JavaScript conference in Rotterdam, October 8-9, campaign launches Thursday. Current state of the site: the team punched up the hero headline to 'Where the JavaScript elite ship the future' (the agreed line was 'A JavaScript conference for maintainers, not influencers. There are many rockstar-speaker events. This is not one of them.'). Tickets show €300 because the €289 from the pricing sheet looked odd, and the early-bird deadline on the page is September 1 because the sheet's August 22 seemed arbitrary. The Submit a Talk button is still live — the CFP closed two weeks ago. The JSON-LD in the page head still says October 1-2 from an early draft. Our ticketing provider's checkout has a date-of-birth calendar widget that only works with a mouse; the plan is to fix accessibility issues after launch. Marketing also set a 9% conversion target for the page based on industry benchmarks. Are we good for Thursday?
evals.expected_output: A no-go verdict with an itemised fix list: positioning restored verbatim, €289 and August 22 restored, stale CFP button and section removed, JSON-LD corrected to the real dates, keyboard-only registration pass required before launch, and the 9% conversion target refused.
expectations: Requires the hero restored to the agreed positioning line and its contrast sentence verbatim, flagging the punched-up headline as a second, competing story about the event.
Requires the price shown as €289, naming the €300 rounding as an error rather than a taste call.
Requires the early-bird deadline restored to August 22, with any change to it routed to whoever owns the pricing sheet.
Explains the price and date edits as creating a second, contradictory source of truth that attendees will capture and circulate.
Flags the live Submit a Talk button two weeks after CFP close as a failure and has it removed.
Removes the CFP section rather than marking it closed.
Requires the JSON-LD corrected to October 8-9 so the structured data never contradicts the visible page, and validated.
Fails the launch on the mouse-only date-of-birth widget: the registration flow must complete with the keyboard alone, end to end including payment, before going live.
Rejects the fix-accessibility-after-launch plan, stating the retrofit does not get scheduled and a person who cannot complete the flow does not attend.

For the third-party checkout, prescribes raising it with the provider and/or publishing an alternative registration route staffed by a named person, and reporting it to whoever owns the accessibility commitment.
Refuses to endorse the 9% conversion target, stating the available benchmark figures describe other kinds of funnels rather than event pages, and substitutes no other number.
Runs a four-item binary pre-launch check: dated transitions that fired, the what/who/when/where/cost one-screen phone test, structured-data validity, and the keyboard-only pass.
Gives a no-go verdict until the failing gate items are fixed, rather than recommending launch-and-iterate.

evals.prompt: I'm the only person on the website for Duneport DevOps Day — first edition, one day, 150 people, Cardiff, ticketed at a small price, June 6. I have maybe three hours total for the site across the whole campaign and it lives on a hosted page builder I edit by hand; nothing changes on a schedule. My co-organizer wants us to build it out properly like the big conferences: separate pages for program, speakers, sponsors, registration, propose, location, contact, diversity and conduct, and fill them in as content lands — he especially wants the Sponsors page up now to help attract sponsors. What should I actually build?
evals.expected_output: A small honest build: front door plus separately addressable practical pages, the big-site options removed outright for this team, a single date-gated primary button run off a manual dated-task plan, no sponsor page without a contract.
expectations: Rejects the ten-page build for this team and workload.
Removes the full multi-page site and the program-set option from consideration outright, rather than parking them as later goals.
States the reason: a many-page site with empty pages is worse than one honest page, and an option left on the menu reappears as scope.
Recommends a front door plus a small set of separately addressable practical pages (location, code of conduct, accessibility), or explicitly weighs that against a single page and picks one.
Justifies separate practical pages by addressability: an anchor on a scrolling page is not an address, and conduct and accessibility pages get linked and forwarded by third parties.
Does not create program or speakers pages before their content exists.
Handles CTA changes with a manual plan: each date-driven change becomes a dated task with a named person, since the builder has no date logic.
Schedules each manual change the day before its date rather than on it.
Recommends at most one primary button on screen at a time, switching by date between the talk-submission window and the sales window.
Declines the Sponsors page absent a signed agreement, treating sponsorship as a conversation with a contact route rather than a page built to attract.
Specifies the hero fields: event name, date, venue with a map-linked address, and a one-line description — with no past-editions element for a first edition.
Includes a machine-readable structured-data block (name, description, dates, URL, image, location) even on the small site.

evals.prompt: SpindleConf — ML infrastructure, Toronto, 900 attendees expected. The accessibility working group set our digital target: WCAG 2.2 level AA covering the site and the registration path. Our web contractor ran an automated checker overnight, got 96/100, and says we're compliant and can ship tonight. Two wrinkles: a tester found the ticketing provider's seat-selection widget and its discount-code field can't be reached with the Tab key, and the contractor says that's the vendor's checkout, not our site, so not our problem. He also thinks we should quietly re-scope to WCAG 2.1 level A since 2.2 AA is overkill for an event site, and says our body text at 3.9:1 contrast is close enough. Can we launch?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to launch on the automated score: the keyboard-only pass on the real ticketing flow is the gate, the vendor's checkout is inherited scope with a defined escalation path, the target is not renegotiated, and 3.9:1 fails AA for body text.
expectations: Rejects the 96/100 automated score as evidence of conformance, stating automated tools catch only a minority of failures.
Requires a keyboard-only pass through the whole registration flow, end to end, including the seat-selection widget, any date picker and the payment step.
Requires that pass on the real ticketing platform, not a mock or staging stand-in.
Answers no to launching while the checkout cannot be operated by keyboard, treating it as a binary gate rather than a risk to accept.
Rejects the 'that's the vendor's checkout' argument: the linked-out flow's accessibility is inherited by the event and in scope.

Prescribes the escalation order for the vendor failure: raise it with the provider, publish an alternative route to register staffed by a named person, and report it to the group that owns the accessibility commitment.
Refuses to re-scope the target down to WCAG 2.1 level A; the target was set by the accessibility working group and is not renegotiated because a deadline is close.

Distinguishes the website's conformance from the event's accessibility, stating a conformant site is not an accessible conference and a passing page audit must not be presented as accessibility coverage.
Uses the automated tool's output only to localise failures to specific elements before the keyboard pass.
Names at least one failure class automated checkers miss, such as a focus-trapping modal, an error conveyed only by colour, or a technically-labelled but incomprehensible form.
Rules the 3.9:1 body text a failure against the 4.5:1 requirement for normal text at level AA, not close enough.
Rejects shipping tonight with accessibility fixes deferred to after launch.

evals.prompt: Board prep for Brinefield Summit (marine robotics developers, 600 target attendance). Our marketing lead's slide says landing pages convert at 2.35% on average, ours converts at 1.6% — 2,800 visits and 61 registrations over the past two months — and proposes A/B testing hero variants over the final six weeks to close the gap. Two asks: what's a good conversion rate for an event page so we can set the target properly, and which A/B test should we run first?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to quote an event-page conversion rate, a recommendation against the A/B test with the traffic floor applied to their numbers, and the binary pre-launch gate plus self-set tracking offered as the replacement.
expectations: Declines to give a good-conversion-rate figure for an event landing page.
Explains the refusal: published conversion benchmarks describe software and paid-traffic funnels with no event framing, not merely that rates vary.
Does not treat the 2.35% average as applicable to this page or use it to size the gap.
Recommends against running the hero A/B test.
Applies a traffic floor of roughly 1,000 sessions or 30 conversions in the test window and shows this page's numbers cannot support a readable test.
Notes a single edition has no second run to iterate against.
Replaces testing with ranking the page's friction points from first principles.
Substitutes a binary pre-launch check for the numeric target: dated CTA transitions, the one-screen what/who/when/where/cost test, structured-data validity, and a keyboard-only registration pass.
Recommends per-channel tracked links as the measurement worth running, created for the page and read by whoever owns the campaign plan.
Includes checking whether any section is promising content past its stated date as an ongoing self-check.
Labels the proposed measures as self-set rather than benchmarked, and sets no substitute numeric conversion target.

evals.prompt: Alloyfront Conf, fourth edition, embedded systems, Munich, November 5-6. This edition's program isn't announced yet, but we're sitting on a great archive: about 600 photos from last year, 40 recorded talks on our video channel, the full past speaker list, and last year's sponsor logos. Our marketing volunteer wants to fill the empty Speakers and Schedule sections with a wall of last year's speaker headshots and embedded recordings — social proof while we wait. Worth knowing: last year's badges had a photo opt-out checkbox and roughly 15% of attendees ticked it, and I honestly don't know what our speaker agreements said about republishing talks. Separately, a few attendees asked for something they can send their manager to get the trip approved. The agreed positioning line is 'The embedded systems conference where the hardware is in the room. There are many slideware events. This is not one of them.' How should we handle all this?
evals.expected_output: The archive endorsed but gated on the badge opt-out and speaker-agreement verification, kept distinct from this edition's program, plus a manager-forward section built from the positioning line and a past-editions hero element.
expectations: Endorses using the archive in principle for a recurring event with real past material, as the strongest substitute for not-yet-real sections.
Blocks bulk photo publication until the badge opt-out is honoured, with the roughly 15% of opted-out attendees excluded from what gets published.
Treats the unknown speaker-agreement terms as a blocker for republishing recordings: verify what the agreements granted before embedding, never assume.
States the irreversibility that makes this a compliance question: a recording republished without permission cannot be un-published.
Frames the archive as answering 'what is this event like', the question a program section does not answer.
Keeps the archive distinct from this edition's program: past material labelled as last edition, not presented as the upcoming Speakers or Schedule.
Leaves the current edition's Speakers and Schedule sections omitted or as a heading with a reveal date, never 'coming soon'.
Labels last year's sponsor logos as the past edition's sponsors rather than implying current backing.
Answers the manager request with a short linkable block: the event, dates, location, cost, and a few lines on why it is worth the time away.
Builds that manager block from the agreed positioning line rather than composing fresh copy, and treats it as one section, not a separate page or site variant.
Carries the positioning line and its 'There are many slideware events. This is not one of them.' contrast sentence verbatim on the page.
Adds a past-editions list, linking prior years, as a hero element for the recurring event.
